strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: as dLLMs gain interest for parallel decoding speedups, a dedicated benchmark exposing the speed-quality trade-off addresses a genuine gap that standard benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) do not capture.

Solid theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 extends the Huang et al. (2022) one-step KL lower bound to T-step parallel decoding via conditional total correlation, and Theorem 2 (with clean proofs of subadditivity and monotonicity, including an input-dependent-partition extension) formally establishes that error grows as parallelism increases. The synthetic list-operation case studies (Copy, Replace Random, Shuffle) yield closed-form C(Y|X) and decoding-strategy accuracy results that are analytically elegant and empirically validated on fine-tuned LLaDA 1.5.

Benchmark design is thoughtfully aligned with theory: tasks span a controlled difficulty spectrum (C(Y|X)=0 tasks like Copy/Sudoku/Replace Index vs. C(Y|X)>0 tasks like Shuffle/Latin Square/W2S), enabling evaluation of whether decoding methods adapt parallelism to task difficulty — a capability no prior benchmark isolates.

Comprehensive experiments: 5 dLLMs (including closed-source Mercury) and 6 autoregressive LLMs, 7+ unmasking strategies, semi-AR decoding, KV caching, fine-tuning, CoT, remasking samplers, and uniform-diffusion variants. The oracle analysis (Section G.2) is a particularly valuable contribution, showing per-sample threshold adaptation leaves substantial headroom.

Empirical findings are interesting and non-obvious in places, e.g., the reversal of difficulty between Replace Index and Replace Random under parallelism, Random Top-k outperforming Confidence Top-k exactly when C(Y|X)>0, and Mercury's failure on Shuffle despite strong Reverse performance.
Paper is clearly written, well-organized, with extensive appendix material (proofs, full results, failure cases) and a released benchmark supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Core theoretical insight is incremental: that conditional independence causes parallel decoding degradation is already known (Wu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025); the main theoretical novelty is generalizing a prior one-step bound to T-step partitions, a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new result.

Theory-to-benchmark connection is partly heuristic: C(Y|X) is computable only for synthetic tasks; for real tasks (W2S, Paraphrasing), claims about relative dependency strength are argued qualitatively ('we argue', 'aligns with expected conditional dependencies') rather than measured, leaving the causal link between C(Y|X) and observed degradation suggestive rather than proven.

Benchmark scale and realism are limited: only ~100 samples per task, very short outputs (32-64 tokens, n<=6 for main Waiting Line results), and 2x2 puzzles. The authors acknowledge this, but it weakens the claim that degradation manifests in 'real-world scenarios'.

Some task results suggest design/evaluation issues: Sort scores near 0 for nearly all models (including Claude Haiku 3.5 at 5.0) despite triviality, and erratic Reverse results, indicating some tasks may measure formatting compliance or evaluation artifacts rather than the intended phenomenon. Grammar scoring via language-tool-python is a crude binary metric.

The 'first benchmark specifically designed for dLLMs' claim is somewhat overstated given prior dLLM-focused evaluations (e.g., Ye et al., 2025a on Countdown/Sudoku) and concurrent analysis work (Gong et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025), which the paper itself discusses.

Practical significance of speed claims is limited: most experiments vary tokens-per-step as a proxy for speed without wall-clock latency measurements; given KV-cache interactions are shown to change results, the speed-quality trade-off framing would benefit from actual throughput measurements.

Several headline conclusions (static parallel decoding degrades quality; adaptive methods are suboptimal; no universally superior unmasking method) are confirmations of anticipated behavior rather than surprising findings, which limits the impact for readers already familiar with the dLLM decoding literature.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: evaluating the speed-quality trade-off of parallel decoding in diffusion LLMs addresses a real gap, since standard benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) under-expose parallel decoding failures.

The theoretical framing is clean: the conditional total correlation lower bound (Theorem 1) and monotonicity result (Theorem 2) are formally stated with proofs, and boundary cases (T=1, T=|Y|) are correctly identified.

The synthetic list-operation case studies are a nice pedagogical device: analytically tractable C(Y|X) values and closed-form accuracy predictions (e.g., 1/e accuracy for Replace Random under sampling) that are empirically validated with fine-tuned LLaDA 1.5.

The benchmark design shows deliberate thought: the Sudoku vs. Latin Square contrast isolates the effect of C(Y|X) > 0 in structurally similar tasks, and the Replace Index vs. Replace Random reversal between one-by-one and parallel decoding is a compelling empirical finding.

Extensive experimental coverage: multiple dLLMs (LLaDA, LLaDA 1.5, Dream 7B, DiffuCoder, Mercury), multiple unmasking strategies, ablations on KV caching, semi-AR block sizes, CoT, remasking samplers, and oracle threshold analysis, with comprehensive results in the appendix.
Honest limitations section acknowledging narrow task coverage and short sequence lengths.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 is essentially a direct application of the chain rule of KL divergence combined with the known one-step bound of Huang et al. (2022); Theorem 2's monotonicity follows from a standard subadditivity argument. Both results formalize intuition rather than providing new machinery or surprising insights.

The core empirical finding — parallel decoding degrades quality when token dependencies are strong — is largely expected and already documented in prior work (Wu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025). The paper's positioning acknowledges this, but the incremental contribution over these works is primarily the benchmark itself.

The 'realistic' benchmark claim is overstated: most tasks are list operations dressed in customer-service templates, and W2S word sets are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro with only 100 samples per task. Small sample sizes raise concerns about statistical reliability of reported accuracies.

A gap between theory and evaluation: the theory bounds KL divergence, but the benchmark measures task accuracy and grammar scores; the link between the KL bound and downstream task metrics is never formalized, so the theory mainly serves as motivation rather than predictive analysis.

The decoding-strategy analysis (Section 4.2) relies on a strongly idealized model (unbiased logits, uniform noise, greedy decoding), and the derived accuracy predictions may not transfer to real dLLMs with calibrated confidence and biased logits; empirical deviations are not systematically analyzed.

Several results are confounded by model capability rather than parallel decoding per se: e.g., Sort scores 0% for all dLLMs and many AR LLMs even with one-by-one decoding, and the paper itself attributes Reverse differences to 'insufficient model capacity.' This weakens the benchmark's ability to cleanly measure parallelism effects.

Only short output sequences (32-64 tokens max) are evaluated, which is precisely the regime where parallel decoding is most attractive; the paper admits longer sequences may yield different conclusions, limiting the practical significance of the headline trade-off findings.

The oracle analysis (Section G.2) shows headroom for adaptive thresholds but offers no method achieving it, so the practical takeaway ('adaptive methods have room for improvement') is fairly thin as an actionable contribution.

Some presentation issues: a 'Project Page' placeholder is left empty, the text-writing evaluation reduces to a binary grammar score in the main body while more informative metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE-L) are relegated to the appendix, and there are minor typos (e.g., 'yield perform similarly').

strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: the paper addresses an important gap in evaluating dLLMs, namely the quality degradation caused by parallel decoding under the conditional independence assumption, which existing standard benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) fail to expose.

The theoretical framing is clean and useful: Theorem 1 extends the total-correlation lower bound (Huang et al., 2022) to T-step parallel decoding, and Theorems 2-3 establish monotonicity of the optimal error bound with the number of decoding steps. Proofs are provided and correct.

The synthetic list-operation case studies are analytically tractable and yield concrete, testable predictions (e.g., C(Y|X) values for Replace Random and Shuffle, accuracy limits for Top-k and Threshold unmasking strategies), which are then empirically validated by fine-tuning LLaDA 1.5, lending credibility to the theory-practice connection.

Extensive empirical evaluation: five dLLMs (including closed-source Mercury), seven autoregressive LLMs, and a broad set of unmasking strategies (Random/Confidence/Left-to-Right/Margin/Entropy Top-k, Confidence Threshold, Factor-based, semi-AR), plus useful supplementary analyses (fine-tuning, CoT, remasking samplers, uniform diffusion, KV caching, oracle analysis).
The oracle speed-quality analysis is a compelling finding showing substantial headroom for adaptive unmasking methods, making the benchmark actionable for future research.

The paper is clearly written, well organized, and includes comprehensive appendix materials (proofs, dataset specifications, prompts, full results, failure cases), supporting reproducibility; the benchmark is stated to be released publicly.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is incremental: Theorem 1 is a fairly direct extension of a known one-step result (Huang et al., 2022) using chain-rule decomposition, and the monotonicity results follow from subadditivity. The novelty of the theory alone would be limited.

Benchmark scope and realism are debatable: 'Waiting Line' tasks are essentially list operations with a thin natural-language veneer, all outputs are very short (32-64 tokens), and each task has only ~100 samples. The paper itself concedes that coverage of real-world scenarios and long-sequence generation is lacking; the central claim that degradation 'persists in real-world scenarios' rests on fairly contrived tasks (queue manipulation, 4-word sentence construction).

Some experiments contain confounds the paper acknowledges but does not fully resolve: e.g., LLaDA scores 0 on Sort even with one-by-one decoding, and Reverse discrepancies are attributed to model capacity rather than token dependencies, weakening the benchmark's diagnostic power for at least some tasks.

The main reported metric for Text Writing is a binary grammar score from an external tool, which is a coarse proxy for generation quality and may not capture the subtler degradation the information-theoretic analysis motivates; no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for the ~100-sample tasks.

The decoding-strategy analysis relies on an idealized unbiased model assumption (task-determined logits plus zero-mean noise); how well the derived accuracy limits transfer to real, biased models is only empirically suggested, not established.

The paper is purely analysis + benchmark: it does not propose or evaluate any new decoding method that improves the trade-off, limiting immediate impact beyond diagnosis; several findings (task-dependent degradation, threshold adaptivity issues) partially overlap with prior work (Wu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025).

Impact on the broader field may be moderate given the specialized scope: the benchmark is specific to dLLM parallel decoding and the tasks are short-form, so adoption beyond the dLLM acceleration sub-community is uncertain.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the speed-quality trade-off of parallel decoding in dLLMs is underexplored, and the paper correctly identifies that standard benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval) fail to expose parallel-decoding failures.

Genuine theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 extends the one-step KL lower bound of Huang et al. (2022) to T-step parallel decoding via conditional total correlation, and Theorem 2 establishes monotonicity of the optimal error bound in the number of steps, with clean proofs (Lemma 1 subadditivity) and a sensible extension to input-dependent partitions.

Analytically tractable case studies (Copy, Replace Index/Random, Shuffle) yield closed-form predictions that are empirically validated on a fine-tuned LLaDA 1.5, connecting data-distribution difficulty (C(Y|X)) and decoding-strategy behavior in a quantitative way.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 dLLMs plus closed-source Mercury, 6 autoregressive LLMs, many unmasking strategies (top-k variants, threshold, factor-based, semi-AR), KV caching, CoT, fine-tuning, remasking samplers (RCR/ReMDM), SEDD variants, Medusa speculative decoding, and recent adaptive methods (SlowFast, DUS, WINO, APD), including an oracle analysis quantifying the headroom for per-sample parallelism adaptation.

Well-designed benchmark structure spanning zero- and high-dependency tasks (Waiting Line, Text Writing, Sudoku vs. Latin Square), which usefully contrasts structurally similar tasks differing only in token dependency; adjustable-length design supports future evaluation.

Thorough appendices: full proofs, dataset specifications, additional metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE-L, inclusion accuracy), longer-output analysis, wall-clock latency measurements, failure cases, and an LLM usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is modest: Theorem 1/2 are direct extensions of existing total-correlation bounds (Huang et al., 2022) to partitioned factorizations, and the main insights (permutation/shuffle tasks are hard for parallel decoding) are largely intuitive.

Benchmark tasks risk being contrived or confounded by model capacity rather than parallelism: e.g., Sort yields 0% accuracy even for strong AR LLMs (Claude Haiku 3.5: 5%), and Sudoku/Insert Index results vary wildly across AR models, making it hard to attribute failures to parallel decoding per se; the authors partially acknowledge this (D.5, Sec. 6), but the primary experiments only use n in {3,4,5,6}, limiting real-world relevance.

Many headline findings are confirmatory/expected (parallel decoding degrades quality on high-dependency tasks; no unmasking method dominates), so the paper's main contribution rests on the benchmark itself rather than surprising science.

Evaluation scale is small: 100 samples per task with binary accuracy yields coarse estimates; grammar scoring via language-tool is a brittle binary metric; several results (e.g., Fig. 5 semi-AR trends) rest on qualitative reading of noisy curves.

Coverage limitations: focus on short outputs (max 32-64 tokens) and small n; longer-sequence behavior, where parallel decoding speedups matter most in practice, is only preliminarily addressed, and uniform-diffusion/SEDD experiments use tiny 90M models not comparable to the 7-8B dLLMs.

Reproducibility: Project Page, Leaderboard, and GitHub fields on the title page are empty at submission time; parts of the benchmark generation rely on Gemini 2.5 Pro outputs without clear verification protocols for task validity (e.g., difficulty tiers of W2S).

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with a logical progression from information-theoretic analysis to synthetic case studies to a realistic benchmark.

Theorem 1 and 2 provide a clean formalization of the parallel decoding quality degradation via conditional total correlation, with correct proofs and a useful monotonicity result connecting the number of decoding steps to the error lower bound.

The synthetic case studies (Shuffle, Replace Random, etc.) are analytically tractable and the derived accuracy expressions (e.g., Eq. 5) are empirically validated with fine-tuned LLaDA 1.5, which strengthens the theoretical claims.

The experimental coverage is extensive: multiple dLLMs (LLaDA, LLaDA 1.5, Dream 7B, DiffuCoder, Mercury), multiple autoregressive baselines, seven unmasking strategies, semi-AR decoding, KV caching, and Medusa-style speculative decoding, showing the benchmark generalizes beyond dLLMs.

The oracle speed-quality analysis (Section F.2, Fig. 7) is a genuinely informative contribution, quantifying headroom for adaptive unmasking methods and showing recent methods (SlowFast, DUS, WINO, APD) remain far from the oracle.
The paper is transparent about limitations (short output lengths, capacity confounds) and includes an LLM usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. The core bound (Eq. 1) is directly from Huang et al. (2022) for one-step generation; Theorem 1 is essentially a chain-rule decomposition of the KL plus this known bound, and Theorem 2's monotonicity follows from a straightforward subadditivity argument. The closed-form analyses in Sections 4.1-4.2 are simple combinatorial calculations rather than deep results.

The 'realistic' framing of the benchmark is questionable. The Waiting Line tasks are synthetic list operations re-wrapped in customer-service language, and Text Writing is limited to 100 samples per task with a coarse binary grammar score from language-tool-python. Tasks of this size yield noisy accuracy estimates, and the customer-service framing does not add realism beyond rephrasing.

There is a significant confound between model capacity and token dependency that the benchmark does not cleanly resolve. The authors themselves admit that Reverse failures stem from 'insufficient model capacity rather than token dependency' (C=0), and in the longer-output setting (D.5) even Copy degrades sharply, meaning many benchmark results conflate capacity limits with the parallel decoding phenomenon the benchmark is meant to isolate.

The claimed positioning as 'the first benchmark specifically designed for dLLMs' overstates novelty. Prior works (Wu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025; Gong et al., 2025) already analyze parallel decoding degradation and speed-quality trade-offs; the incremental contribution is primarily the design of dependency-controlled tasks rather than the evaluation methodology.

The main practical findings (parallel decoding degrades quality on dependency-heavy tasks; adaptive strategies outperform static ones; a gap to oracle remains) are somewhat anticipated by the cited literature and largely confirm what the community already suspects, limiting the significance of the conclusions.

Several evaluation details raise concerns: the adaptive analysis depends heavily on threshold hyperparameter sweeps; one-shot prompting choices and exact-match accuracy on highly formatted outputs may penalize dLLMs for formatting rather than reasoning; and only a single representative open-source dLLM is analyzed in depth in the main text.

Broader impact on real workloads is unclear: tasks are short (32-64 tokens) and, as the authors concede, longer-sequence behavior is confounded by capacity, so the relevance of the findings to production dLLM usage remains open.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—the speed-quality trade-off of parallel decoding in diffusion LLMs is underexplored and poorly captured by standard benchmarks, and this motivation is convincingly argued throughout.

The information-theoretic analysis is clean and rigorous: Theorem 1 gives a KL lower bound via conditional total correlation for T-step parallel decoding, Theorem 2 establishes monotonicity of the optimal bound, and the proofs (Appendix A) are correct and the definitions are standard and clearly stated.

The synthetic list-operation case studies are analytically tractable and yield crisp, quantitative predictions (e.g., Shuffle accuracy converging to 0, Replace Random achieving 1/e under sampling), which are then empirically validated with fine-tuned LLaDA 1.5—a nice theory-to-practice loop.

ParallelBench is well-designed: it spans a spectrum of token-dependency levels (tasks with C(Y|X)=0 vs. C(Y|X)>0), is grounded in realistic scenarios (queue management, text writing, puzzles), and includes clever contrasts such as Sudoku (unique solution) vs. Latin Square (many solutions) to isolate the effect of C(Y|X).

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a benchmark paper: 5 dLLMs, 5 autoregressive LLMs, multiple unmasking strategies, KV caching, semi-AR decoding, fine-tuning, CoT, remasking samplers, SEDD variants, Medusa, wall-clock latency measurements, longer-output analysis, and an oracle analysis quantifying headroom for adaptive parallelism.

The findings are actionable and clearly stated (static top-k fails, threshold methods have a large gap to oracle), and the benchmark's adjustable difficulty (n parameter) makes it forward-compatible with stronger future models. Reproducibility appears good, with detailed appendix, prompts, hyperparameters, and an LLM usage disclosure.

The paper is honest about limitations: confounds between model capacity and parallel decoding effects on longer outputs are explicitly acknowledged and partially mitigated by design choices (small n).
weaknesses: Benchmark scale is small: only 100 samples per task and 17 tasks total, with several tasks (list operations) being synthetic and templated. The 'realistic' framing of Waiting Line is thin—renaming list operations as customer-service scenarios does not fully bridge the gap to real-world LLM usage, and the paper's claim that degradation 'extends beyond synthetic to real-world scenarios' is only partially supported.

The grammar-score-based evaluation for Text Writing relies on a single external tool (language-tool-python), which is a coarse binary metric; human or LLM-judge evaluation would strengthen the claim of quality degradation in free-form generation.

Most headline results in the main text focus on a single model (LLaDA 1.5), and per-sample variance, confidence intervals, and number of decoding seeds are not consistently reported; some accuracy differences across unmasking methods in the figures appear small relative to plausible run-to-run noise.

There are confounds the theory does not fully disentangle: degraded accuracy under parallelism can arise from (i) the intrinsic C(Y|X) bound, (ii) model capacity limitations, and (iii) training-inference mismatch of masked diffusion models. The paper attributes results to (i) via the theory, but the empirical models are far from the ideal-model assumptions, and tasks like Reverse (C=0 yet poor under parallelism) show this confound persists.

Novelty is moderate: the core observation (conditional independence in parallel decoding causes factorization error) is known, and prior works (Wu et al. 2025; Feng et al. 2025; Gong et al. 2025) already analyze related degradation. The contribution is primarily a well-executed consolidation plus a new benchmark, rather than a fundamentally new insight or method.

The oracle analysis, while informative, defines an upper bound via per-sample threshold selection using knowledge of correctness—an idealization that could overstate attainable gains, and its relation to practically realizable adaptive strategies is not analyzed in depth.

Some analysis choices are heuristic (e.g., 'center of mass' metric for parallelizability, slope fitting for order preference in Fig. 6) without sensitivity analysis, and the taxonomy tables label dependency levels ('Medium', 'Very High') without formal definitions or computed C(Y|X) values for the benchmark tasks.
